strengths: The submission addresses a timely and important evaluation gap. UniREditBench contains 2,700 examples balanced across 18 subcategories, covering both realistic transformations/interactions and rule-based game tasks that are underrepresented in prior editing benchmarks.
Providing a textual description and reference image for every example is potentially useful for evaluating complex edits that cannot be specified unambiguously through short text alone.

The programmatic generation of game states and solutions offers stronger logical correctness guarantees than purely generative construction, while the final inspection by eight annotators is a valuable quality-control step.

The empirical coverage is broad, including multiple open- and closed-source editors and detailed category-level results. Fine-tuning Bagel on the proposed 100,421-example dataset produces large in-domain gains and improvements on the external RISEBench and KRISBench benchmarks.
The taxonomy, synthesis pipeline, scoring dimensions, and qualitative examples are presented clearly. The accompanying training dataset could be valuable beyond the benchmark itself.
weaknesses: The central claim that dual-reference evaluation is more reliable is not adequately validated. The paper provides only an illustrative example and reports no human-rating study, human–evaluator correlation, ranking agreement, text-only-versus-dual-reference ablation, or comparison across independent VLM judges. Consequently, all main benchmark conclusions depend on an unverified GPT-4.1 evaluator.

A single reference image can itself introduce false negatives because many real-world edits admit multiple visually valid outcomes. The manuscript does not examine whether the evaluator over-penalizes outputs that satisfy the instruction but differ from the synthesized reference, nor does it quantify this ambiguity by category.

The nominally real-world portion is entirely synthetic: prompts are expanded by Gemini, image pairs are generated by GPT-4o, and filtering/CoT generation again relies on Gemini. This creates correlated generator and judge biases, may favor outputs resembling the synthetic reference distribution, and weakens claims about performance on genuine real-image editing. GPT-4o is also evaluated on a benchmark whose real-world reference images it generated, a potential source-model advantage that is not analyzed.

Separation between UniREdit-Data-100K and UniREditBench is insufficiently documented. Both use the same taxonomy and synthesis pipelines, while no cross-set image, instruction, template, or semantic-overlap audit is reported. The exceptionally large in-domain gains of UniREdit-Bagel, especially on game tasks, therefore cannot be cleanly distinguished from narrow distribution or template matching.

The claimed value of high-quality CoT supervision is unsupported by ablations. There is no comparison against training on the same image pairs without CoT, against generic rationales, or across dataset sizes, so the improvements establish the utility of the overall dataset but not the specific reasoning-supervision claim.

Human curation is underspecified: the paper omits annotator qualifications, per-item redundancy, agreement statistics, rejection/correction rates, and category-wise quality audits. Automated filtering is also performed by essentially the same model family used during data construction, without independent validation.

Reproducibility information is incomplete. The displayed project-page field is blank, and the manuscript gives no concrete release/access information for the benchmark, data, code, evaluator prompts, or game programs. Exact API/model versions and inference settings are unclear, while training details omit batch size, hardware, random seeds, loss weights, and uncertainty across runs.

The results contain no confidence intervals, repeated evaluations, or sensitivity analysis for stochastic generation and VLM judging. Given several relatively close model scores, it is unclear which ranking differences are statistically or practically robust. Overall, the benchmark is promising, but the missing validation of its evaluation mechanism and synthetic-domain biases slightly outweigh its scale and scope.

strengths: The work addresses a timely problem: evaluating instruction-based image editing that requires physical, temporal, spatial, and rule-based reasoning rather than simple attribute changes.

Treating this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution is more appropriate than the default Algorithms/General category. Under that framing, the proposed 2,700-example benchmark, paired visual/text references, 100K-example training set, and coverage of both real-world and game-world tasks constitute a potentially useful resource.

The evaluation includes numerous open- and closed-source systems, category-level results, qualitative comparisons, and tests on two external benchmarks. UniREdit-Bagel's improvements on RISEBench and KRISBench provide some evidence that the training data transfers beyond the proposed benchmark.
Programmatic generation of game states can provide exact rule-governed targets, while the filtering pipeline combines automated checks with inspection by eight annotators.
weaknesses: The central claim that dual-reference evaluation is more reliable is not adequately validated. The paper provides one illustrative example but no human-evaluator study, agreement statistics, comparison of text-only versus dual-reference rankings, or correlation analysis against human judgments. Since nearly every quantitative conclusion depends on GPT-4.1-as-judge, this is a consequential omission.

A single reference image is not necessarily ground truth for open-ended real-world editing: many visually different outputs can correctly satisfy an instruction. The proposed evaluator may reward resemblance to the particular synthetic target and penalize valid alternatives. This issue is neither measured nor discussed.

Benchmark and training data are generated through the same pipeline and taxonomy, but the manuscript does not establish cross-set deduplication or otherwise demonstrate that UniREditBench is disjoint from UniREdit-Data-100K. Consequently, the very large in-domain gains of UniREdit-Bagel may reflect generator/style or template leakage rather than general reasoning ability. External results help, but remain substantially below the strongest closed systems and are evaluated with the same unvalidated judge.

The dataset itself is characterized insufficiently for a benchmark contribution. There is no reporting of acceptance rates, source-prompt counts, annotation protocol details, inter-annotator agreement, correction frequency, train/test similarity, demographic or content composition, or systematic audit of target correctness. Requiring a proprietary VLM score of 5 on every filtering dimension does not independently establish quality.

The taxonomy and reporting are internally inconsistent. Section 3 describes two real-world primary dimensions plus four game-world dimensions, while the paper repeatedly claims eight primary dimensions and Tables 2/5 introduce four differently named real-world groups without explaining their mapping. Score conversion from the stated 1–5 ratings to the approximately 0–100 table values is also unspecified.

The experimental evidence lacks evaluator ablations, training-data-size ablations, CoT-versus-no-CoT comparisons, comparison against fine-tuning on matched data without reasoning traces, uncertainty estimates, and repeated evaluations. Thus the paper cannot support its claim that CoT annotations specifically improve reasoning or that reported model differences are statistically reliable.

Reproducibility is weak: key generation prompts, GPT-4.1 judging rubric, randomization and decoding settings, exact model/API versions, benchmark split construction, and release details are absent. Several named baselines are listed but not reported in the main comparison. The project-page placeholder contains no usable URL.

Attribution contains concerning errors. The cited “Game-RL” reference used to motivate game-code synthesis is a malware-generation paper, and the GPT-4.1 evaluator is cited using the GPT-4o system card. These are not merely stylistic citation issues because they obscure the provenance of central methodology and evaluation choices.

The ethical statement simply asserts that no concerns exist. It does not address dependence on proprietary services, generated-data licensing and terms, representational bias, potentially violent synthetic content, benchmark misuse, or the risks of releasing chain-of-thought-style synthetic supervision.

strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, this submission is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks. UniREditBench is a substantial and timely resource: 2,700 human-inspected examples cover 18 reasoning categories across real- and game-world editing, including multi-object interactions and rule-governed tasks that are underrepresented in prior benchmarks.

The dual-reference evaluation idea is well motivated. Providing both a textual description of the intended effect and a ground-truth edited image can expose errors that a text-only evaluator may miss, especially for paths, puzzles, and spatially precise edits.

The empirical scope is strong: the paper evaluates numerous open- and closed-source systems, reports category-level results, provides many qualitative comparisons, and tests UniREdit-Bagel on two external benchmarks. Its 18.3% RISEBench score improves substantially over Bagel-Think's 9.2%, while its 65.45 KRISBench score also improves on the 60.77 baseline.

UniREdit-Data-100K is balanced across categories and combines automated filtering with inspection by eight annotators. Fine-tuning Bagel yields large gains on UniREditBench, particularly for game-world reasoning, demonstrating the practical utility of the collected data.

The manuscript is generally clear, visually effective, and well organized; the taxonomy, synthesis pipelines, and representative task examples are easy to understand. weaknesses: The central claim that dual-reference evaluation is more reliable is supported mainly by one illustrative example. There is no human-correlation study, evaluator ablation comparing text-only and dual-reference variants, inter-rater analysis, or robustness test across multiple VLM judges. This is the most important missing validation for a benchmark paper.

The benchmark and training set are generated by closely related pipelines, and the real-world images rely heavily on GPT-4o while filtering and evaluation rely on closely related proprietary VLMs. The paper does not quantify template or semantic overlap between UniREdit-Data-100K and UniREditBench. Consequently, the very large in-domain gain may partly reflect generator/style or task-template alignment rather than general reasoning improvement; the more modest external-benchmark gains reinforce this concern.

The paper attributes improved reasoning to chain-of-thought supervision without comparing against the same fine-tuning data with CoT removed, hidden, or replaced by direct supervision. Data-size and category-mixture ablations are also absent, so the respective effects of more data, task distribution, and explicit reasoning traces cannot be separated.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The evaluator prompt and full scoring rubric are not provided; the reported 1–5 scores are apparently rescaled in the tables without explanation; key training details such as batch size, resolution, loss weights, and compute are missing; and proprietary baseline versions, access dates, sampling settings, and repeated-run variability are insufficiently documented.

The human-inspection claim needs more evidence: the manuscript gives no per-item annotation redundancy, acceptance/rejection rates, annotator qualifications beyond calling them experts, agreement statistics, or audit results. This limits confidence in the benchmark's asserted ground-truth quality.

The ethical statement is too cursory for a dataset intended for release. It does not discuss licensing and redistribution rights for proprietary-model outputs, possible synthetic-data biases, annotation labor, or limitations arising from dependence on commercial APIs.

strengths: This is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. The paper targets an important gap in reasoning-intensive image editing and substantially broadens coverage beyond simple attribute changes, particularly through multi-object physical interactions and rule-governed game tasks.

The benchmark is sizeable, with 2,700 samples across 18 stated categories, and every instance includes an input, instruction, textual reference, and reference image. Programmatic generation of game states and solutions is especially valuable because it can provide exact rule-based supervision.

The dual-reference evaluation idea is intuitive and potentially useful. The authors do not rely solely on anecdotal evidence: they compare reference configurations against human judgments and report lower error when both text and images are supplied to the evaluator.
The empirical coverage is broad, including numerous open- and closed-source editors, category-level results, two VLM judges, qualitative failure analysis, and evaluation on RISEBench and KRISBench.

UniREdit-Data-100K and the fine-tuned UniREdit-Bagel show large improvements over Bagel, including gains on external benchmarks. This suggests that the proposed data may provide useful supervision beyond direct benchmark memorization.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes substantial supplementary material on filtering, game rules, scaling, transfer, and qualitative results.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not sufficiently independent of the training pipeline. UniREdit-Bagel is trained on data produced from the same synthesis process, categories, rendering conventions, and likely prompt templates as UniREditBench. The paper does not clearly document benchmark/training deduplication, template separation, generator separation, or contamination checks. Consequently, the very large in-domain gain—especially on game tasks—may reflect distribution and rendering familiarity rather than general reasoning ability. External results help, but UniREdit-Bagel still trails the strongest closed models substantially on RISEBench.

Reference-image judging introduces an inadequately studied bias. Many real-world instructions admit multiple correct visual outcomes, so similarity to one synthetic reference can penalize valid edits. It may also favor a model trained on images from the same generator and style. The paper reports aggregate human agreement but does not separately test alternative-valid outputs, evaluator preference for reference style, or rank changes relative to human model rankings.

The human validation is too limited and underspecified for a benchmark whose conclusions depend heavily on VLM scores. Only 200 randomly selected samples and four models are mentioned; the paper omits per-category sampling, score aggregation across six experts, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, significance tests, and human-based model rankings. An average MAE of 0.44–0.64 on a five-point scale does not by itself establish reliable ranking, and the error varies by evaluated model.

Several definitions and reported quantities are internally unclear. The taxonomy claims eight primary dimensions, while Sec. 3.2 explicitly describes two real-world groups plus four game-world dimensions; Tables 2 and 7 regroup the real-world categories into four differently named aggregates without explaining the mapping. The scoring equations produce values from 1 to 5, whereas the result tables report roughly 0–100 scores without defining the conversion.

Key ablations do not support the associated causal claims. There is no controlled comparison of identical training data with versus without CoT supervision, while Table 10 merely asks another VLM whether CoTs contain causal language and whether outputs align with them. The game-data transfer ablation appears confounded by training-set size, and the weight-selection correlations differ only marginally without uncertainty estimates. No repeated runs or error bars are reported.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate for a benchmark paper. The project-page field is blank, and the manuscript does not provide the benchmark/data link, full evaluator prompts, image-generation and decoding settings, exact API/model snapshots, train/test construction rules, image resolutions, annotation workload, annotator agreement, or complete filtering statistics. The baseline list in Sec. 5.1 also does not match the models appearing in the main result table.

The real-world benchmark is itself synthetically generated and filtered by related proprietary VLMs, which limits ecological validity and creates correlated generator/evaluator errors. The paper lacks comparison against a substantial set of naturally sourced photographs or independently produced target edits.

Some game tasks measure a mixture of visual perception, symbolic planning, coordinate interpretation, and precise raster redrawing. Without oracle-rendered action evaluation or separate reasoning-versus-rendering diagnostics, failures cannot confidently be attributed to reasoning, and the benchmark's interpretation as image-editing ability is partly confounded.

The ethical statement is cursory. It claims no ethical concerns despite reliance on proprietary generators and evaluators and a planned dataset release; licensing, generated-content provenance, representational bias, misuse, and privacy safeguards are not addressed. Overall, the benchmark is promising, but these validity and reproducibility concerns currently shift the close decision slightly toward rejection.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, the paper is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General. Under that framing, covering 2,700 examples across 18 categories—including multi-object physical interactions and rule-governed game tasks—is potentially useful and broader than the cited reasoning-editing benchmarks.

Providing both textual descriptions and reference images is a sensible attempt to improve VLM-based evaluation. The comparison against text-only and image-only reference settings, together with a six-expert study on 200 samples, is directionally supportive.
The benchmark includes a reasonably broad set of open- and closed-source editors and reports category-level results, revealing substantial weaknesses on strategic, logical, and long-horizon tasks.
The programmatic generation of game states and answers is appropriate for tasks with deterministic rules and should provide more reliable targets than purely generative synthesis.

The paper is generally well organized and visually polished, with helpful taxonomies, rules, qualitative comparisons, out-of-distribution evaluations, scaling results, and filtering details in the supplement.
weaknesses: The central dual-reference premise is not adequately justified for open-ended real-world edits. These reference images are GPT-4o-generated realizations, not ground truth observations, and many instructions admit multiple equally correct appearances. Comparing an output against one arbitrary generated realization can penalize valid edits or reward superficial resemblance; the paper demonstrates only one favorable maze example and does not quantify this reference-induced bias separately for deterministic and open-ended tasks.

Benchmark independence is unclear. UniREditBench and UniREdit-Data-100K are produced through the same pipelines, categories, generators, and likely prompt templates, after which UniREdit-Bagel is trained on the 100K dataset and evaluated on the benchmark. No train-test deduplication protocol, template split, generator split, or similarity analysis is reported. Consequently, the very large in-domain gains—especially the near-saturated game scores—may reflect distribution or template matching rather than general reasoning.

The evaluator validation is too limited for a benchmark whose conclusions depend almost entirely on VLM judgments. The 200-sample study does not report sampling stratification, whether 200 denotes total examples or examples per model, per-expert workload, inter-rater agreement, uncertainty, significance, or full evaluation prompts. An average MAE below one on a five-point scale is not by itself strong validation. Figure 7 also lacks numerical results and uncertainty estimates.

Evaluation design choices appear tuned and tested using the same small human study. The score weights are selected for maximum correlation on those judgments, but no held-out validation set is used; several candidate weight triples do not sum to one, and the paper does not clearly explain how 1–5 component ratings become the 0–100 values in the main tables. These omissions weaken interpretability and reproducibility.

The real-world benchmark and training data are heavily model-generated: Gemini expands and filters prompts, GPT-4o synthesizes both image endpoints, and GPT-4.1 performs the main evaluation. This creates correlated generator/judge biases and makes claims of 'ground-truth' images and systematic physical reasoning too strong. Validation by an independent evaluator is only reported as similar scoring trends, not as agreement with human rankings or correctness.

The human data-quality process is underspecified despite being central to the claimed reliability. The paper does not state annotation redundancy, agreement or adjudication, category-specific rejection rates, annotator qualifications beyond 'experts,' or whether every one of the roughly 103K benchmark and training instances was independently inspected. Requiring a VLM score of exactly five on six criteria is also not validated as an effective quality filter.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark/data contribution. Important details such as complete generation and judge prompts, random seeds, API/model snapshots, decoding settings, image resolution, batch size, compute, per-baseline preprocessing, licensing, and an explicit release plan are missing. The baseline list is also inconsistent with the models actually appearing in the tables.

The benchmark aggregates natural-image editing with game-board annotation and symbolic puzzle execution, which are materially different capabilities. Equal category counts and a single overall average are not sufficiently motivated, so model rankings may depend on an arbitrary task mixture. Overall, these validity and independence concerns are consequential enough that the current experiments do not establish a trustworthy benchmark, despite the promising scope.

strengths: Best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. UniREditBench addresses an important gap by expanding reasoning-based image-editing evaluation beyond single-object transformations to multi-object physical interactions and rule-governed game scenarios. Its 2,700 examples span 8 primary dimensions and 18 sub-dimensions, with 150 inspected examples per sub-dimension.

The dual-reference protocol is a useful and intuitive contribution: combining a textual description with a target image can expose state inconsistencies that a text-only judge misses. The paper supports this design with a six-expert study on 200 samples, reference-modality ablations, and weight selection based on correlation with human judgments.

The empirical scope is strong. The benchmark covers numerous open- and closed-source editors, reports category-level results with two evaluators, and provides informative qualitative examples and failure analyses, including object deletion and duplication in rule-based environments.

UniREdit-Data-100K and UniREdit-Bagel add value beyond evaluation alone. Fine-tuning produces large in-domain gains and meaningful out-of-distribution improvements over Bagel-Think on RISEBench and KRISBench, supporting the usefulness of the synthesized supervision rather than only benchmark specialization.

The benchmark construction is reasonably thoughtful: game-world targets are programmatically generated; real-world data undergo automated checks and two-stage human inspection; and the supplement describes quality filtering, semantic deduplication, scaling behavior, game-data transfer, and CoT analysis. The paper is generally clear and visually well presented.
weaknesses: A single reference image is not necessarily ground truth for inherently multimodal real-world edits. Multiple physically plausible outcomes, poses, or appearances may satisfy an instruction, so image-conditioned judging can penalize valid alternatives or reward superficial resemblance. The human study is encouraging but does not separately establish this validity across deterministic game tasks and ambiguous real-world tasks.

The relationship between UniREdit-Data-100K and the 2,700-example benchmark needs much stronger leakage analysis. Both are produced from the same taxonomy and synthesis pipelines, while the reported deduplication appears to address redundancy within generated real-world data rather than train-test similarity. Near-duplicate scenes, instructions, templates, or game states could inflate UniREdit-Bagel's large in-domain advantage. Explicit cross-split template, semantic, and image-similarity audits are needed.

The evaluator validation is under-specified. The paper does not clearly report how the 200 samples are distributed across categories and models, how six experts' judgments are aggregated, inter-annotator agreement, uncertainty or confidence intervals, or statistical significance. The same human judgments also appear to inform weight selection and evaluation-protocol validation, raising a possible tuning-on-validation concern.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the displayed project-page field is blank, and exact judge prompts/rubrics, API versions, inference dates, random seeds, sampling settings, training hardware, batch size, and complete benchmark-generation templates are not provided. Results relying on changing proprietary editors and GPT-4.1 evaluation may therefore be difficult to reproduce.

The real-world benchmark images and references are themselves synthetically produced and filtered largely by proprietary models. This may introduce generator-specific aesthetics, causal priors, and evaluator bias, limiting conclusions about editing natural user photographs. A stratified analysis on independently sourced or human-edited real images would materially strengthen the generality claim.

The ethical statement is too cursory for a released 100K-example generative dataset and model. It should discuss licensing and permitted redistribution of generated outputs, biases inherited from proprietary generators and judges, possible misuse of the fine-tuned editor, and the rationale for releasing detailed model-generated reasoning traces.
